questions.prompt: What range of values can an 8-bit two's complement number represent?
questions.explanation: Eight bits give 256 patterns. Two's complement has exactly one zero, so the range is not symmetric: it runs from -128 up to +127.

questions.prompt: How do you negate a two's complement number?
options: Flip the sign bit
Flip every bit
Flip every bit, then add one
Subtract it from 255
questions.explanation: Flipping every bit gives the one's complement; adding one gives two's complement. Flipping only the sign bit is sign-and-magnitude, which is a different representation.

questions.prompt: What decimal value does the 8-bit two's complement pattern 11111111 represent?
questions.explanation: Flip the bits to get 00000000, add one to get 00000001 = 1, so the original is -1. All-ones is -1 in two's complement at any width, which is why it is a handy mask.

questions.prompt: Why does two's complement let the same adder circuit do subtraction?
options: Because subtraction is detected by the control unit and routed elsewhere
Because a - b is computed as a + (-b), and negation is cheap
Because the sign bit is ignored during addition
Because the carry out is discarded
questions.explanation: This is the whole reason the representation won. Negating is flip-and-add-one, which is a row of inverters and a carry-in of 1, so one adder handles both operations and no separate subtractor is needed.

questions.prompt: Adding the 8-bit two's complement numbers 01111111 and 00000001 gives 10000000. What has happened?
options: Nothing unusual: the result is 128
Signed overflow: two positives produced a negative
A carry out of the top bit, which is always an error
Underflow, because the result is too small
questions.explanation: 127 + 1 cannot fit in eight signed bits, so the result wraps to -128. The giveaway is the sign: adding two positive numbers must give a positive number, and it did not. Note there is no carry out of the top bit here - overflow and carry are different flags.

questions.prompt: An 8-bit value 10110100 is copied into a 16-bit register. What should the top eight bits be set to if the value is signed?
options: All zeros, because the value is being widened
All ones, copying the sign bit
The same byte repeated
Whatever was already in the register
questions.explanation: This is sign extension. The value is negative, so the sign bit of 1 is copied across the new high bits to preserve it. Filling with zeros instead would turn a small negative number into a large positive one - the classic bug when a signed byte is widened as if it were unsigned.
